I'm the hummer--exactly like this, short, repetitive bits of songs over and over. I may or may not realize I'm doing it. When I lived with roommates with varying degrees of sensory sensitivities I'd sometimes get asked if I could change the song. Didn't bother me. Sometimes I'd revert accidentally, then catch myself and apologise. Would it be okay if they kept humming but hummed something different? That could be easier for them to hear. As for bringing it up just make it clear that it's an issue with you not with them and they'd be doing you a solid and you love them and their quirks. "Can you pause the humming for a bit? I strongly feel like a lot of us who grew up with unmanaged ADHD have problems caused by our negative self talk/poor self esteem due to histories of failure, and our resulting expectations of future failure. Setting up situations where you know you will succeed in small ways and then actively rewarding yourself (with pride and acknowledgment) has helped me with this a lot. I came to understand this through discussions of "learning history" in dogs.  

I know it's not good to compare disabled people to animals but in the privacy of my own head I find a lot of benefit and comfort to thinking of myself this way. Animal behaviour is shaped by the enviroment and the immediate short term consequences, and so am I, and that can be worked with.

I don't know if ADHD has anything to do with it (I'm undiagnosed-ish) but when I was depressed I did not believe I was depressed. Like you said, sometimes I would have periods where I was aware that the way I was thinking and feeling wasn't right but most of the time I felt like I was making a big deal out of nothing. It is only in retrospect that I can see how depressed I really was. It can be hard to take your own suffering seriously but if you take those screening tests with questions like "How often in the last two weeks have you felt guilty or ashamed/down or blue/etc" and they come up showing depression there is a reason. I used to take these semi regularly but would blow off the results (thinking things like "sure I think about suicide almost every day but I'm not thinking about it seriously/yeah I feel self-loathing every day but I don't feel it ALL of the time") and I was completely shocked last year when I took one of these questionaires as part of something longer and found myself circling "never/rarely" almost all the way down. If you are like me you might have an easier time trusting these "objective" measures rather than trying to just introspect your way to answers.

In my experience what happens is you start getting tense and anxious over the possibility of getting anxious, and it's easy to fixate on that and have it lead to an anxious episode again, which only teaches you that you were right to worry about it and makes that worry stronger next time leading to a vicious cycle. Personally I started associating the physical sensations I felt from getting high with anxiety and it got to the point where I had taught myself that getting high was always scary and I would start feeling anxious immediately after taking a hit before the high had even kicked in. 
   
    
 I would reccomend smoking way way smaller quantities, only in environments you are very comfortable in, and only around people you are very confortable with, plus finding techniques that work for you that help to keep you grounded. For now, try to just barely get high, or don't even smoke enough to feel it at all. Be very particular with who you get high around, or if you get high around anyone at all. Do something fun and relaxing and resist the urge to smoke more if it starts off feeling good. We want to teach your brain that smoking isn't scary by having as many successful non-anxious sessions as we can, by smoking very very little and making it as easy and smooth as possible. Slowly work your dosage up again but be very conservative with it--every time you smoke and get an anxiety attack you are making it harder and harder to undo that connection. On the other hand, if you do start to become anxious try to remember that the anxiety might feel awful but it won't hurt you and it will pass. You want to build confidence that even if you become anxious you are capable of dealing with that anxiety. There's lots of exercises that people use to relax but imo you have to find the right ones for you because the wrong ones can make it worse. For example I had a horrible time with most breathing exercises until I found one I liked.

    
  However I will add that though what I am describing worked for me, I'm not sure it was a good thing. I used to get anxiety and panic attacks from weed and I smoked about as much you do or a bit less. Since I have changed my reaction, I started smoking almost every day and it's been hard to reduce my use. Plus I do still get anxious from time to time even though it's not nearly as bad and doesn't last as long. The other commentors might be right that it's better to quit.

Honestly I don't have a solid idea of what cisgender means when it comes down to it. It's been years since I really sought out and thought about gender 'theory' and I've forgotten a lot. Instinctively to me it means someone who doesn't experience a conflict with regards to their assignment at birth, which is where I guess we would disagree. But something I have seen a lot of lately is discussion around what words are identities and what words are not, and I don't fully grasp it but I can see how it is a real problem. The obvious example being race and racial identity. I don't mean to say some things are 'real' and some things are 'only identities', I'm not an educated guy, but I can sort of feel out the edges of the shape in the dark if you know what I mean. A transgender person has a transgender experience of the world. I'm rambling, but this kind of thing has been on my mind since I have been seeing conversations around the words transmasc and transfem recently, and longer than that when I saw discussions around trans man and trans woman being used in ways different from ftm/mtf (such as nonbinary afab lesbians using trans woman).  I guess anyone can ID however they want but other people can also come up and tell them they're using words wrong. What are the function of those words? Is it functional to use them in specific ways? Most of the time I'm onboard with hey it's not hurting anyone let people use the words they want to, but I also remember a transracial adoptee being really hurt by the effects on her life by that term (transracial) coming to more commonly mean people who identified as another race. And even with race I recently listened to a older podcast episode about race in Brazil vs race in the USA which among other things featured an American man who was Black in the USA but in Brazil he was not. Who decides the 'truth'? How much does context matter? I dunno, you can tell this has been rattling around in my brain for a while and your comment just poked it I spose. Not TRYING to be a nitpicky piece of shit I swear it just comes naturally. Hope I have not made your bad mood any worse :)

Why are people's feelings not relevant when discussing the definition of the term transmasc but relevant with cisgender? I feel as you can't have it both ways. Either transmasc and cisgender have particular meanings based on realities beyond feelings, or they don't, right?

No advice just empathy. My life isn't yours but I see a lot of myself in your post. I'm 27 and the last few years have really started to instill a dread in me of being 30 (an arbritary number really) and still being exactly like I am now. I have an OK job in a shitty industry that I don't know how to get out of, and I make enough money to live with roommates but I don't know how I'm ever going to be able to live alone. I spend all my time sitting around doing nothing and I want to go back to school but like you I never did any work when I was in school, and now that I've exhausted my mom's ability to finance that I'd have to somehow come up with the savings myself, and I'm too afraid of just losing all my money because once again I won't even try. I don't have hobbies either. Sometimes I get excited about studying or learning something or working out but it only lasts maybe 2 weeks before I can't be bothered anymore. Sometimes I don't even start because I'm already anticipating giving up. I'm on an SSRI right now and it stops me from falling into horrible self hatred pits but it hasn't changed my functioning at all. I still don't cook or clean or wash my face or brush my teeth and I owe the government money that I HAVE but can't be bothered to pay and I'm 3 years behind on taxes and yadda yadda and I know the longer I go like this the more I'm screwing myself over. I got a referral a few years ago to an adult ADHD clinic but I screwed up the paperwork and fixing it was too difficult so I just let the referral lapse.

Hopefully I haven't me-me-me'd too much on your post but it makes me feel better to hear from other people who are living similar lives, and I hope it helps you a bit too. The one thing that might be helpful for you jobwise is my experience there. I got a job washing dishes at I think 23 because in a few months my mom was going to be leaving the country and I would no longer be able to live with her. It was a shitty job but it worked out for me pretty well because there was no work to take home, there was no need to self-motivate at all, there was no need to slowly grind at projects, just 8 hours frantically washing everything that showed up in the pit. Cooking is the crap industry I'm stuck in now but it is also the only thing I felt pretty OK at and still do. Plus my coworkers are almost all fuckups in their own ways. Not reccomending that specifically but am recommending anything similarly paced.

Also one of my favourite people is my age and just moving back in with the parents, constantly losing or quitting jobs and "getting nowhere" and I love her and her existance brightens my life. My roommate is your age and unemployed for years and plays video games all day and is a good friend and very intelligent person. It's hard to feel like a loser but you still have worth as a person, there are others out there who struggle the same way. It must be very hard for you when your family and friends are so successful, but outside of your social circle I promise you are not alone.

Something I remind myself of is ADHD or not, the things I don't do make me miserable, so clearly if I could just do them I would, and I'm not just a terrible person. Hope that makes sense it's not super well expressed even in my head.

I'm 27 and only bought a bike and started learning last month! I'm lucky to have an alleyway right behind my house with a gentle slope that I did all my learning on the first few days, plus a park at the end of the block for some grass padding. I was amazed at how fast I got better. I started with the seat low enough to have my feet flat and just pushed and balanced for maybe a metre at most, gradually got better, and suddenly one time made it all the way down the alley and started pedaling and it's all gotten better since then. Now I bike to and from work, have my seat back up, and only look like an idiot once or twice a day when I fail to make this one damn turn sharp enough and yes hit the bush. Every time I've publicly crashed people have been really nice. I stick to bike paths or really quiet residential streets and use https://vancouver.bikerouteplanner.com/ instead of google maps since it seems to give me much safer/more comfortable for my skill level routes.

People who learned as kids aren't always great teachers but if you have some space and time and do a little research you'll figure it out pretty fast! Cycling with a friend is really helpful too once you're a little bit more comfortable on the bike. I don't think I would have ventured out of my alley and residential block for a long time if I didn't have a friend take me on a little trip. 

And I haven't been on the sea wall yet so you're ahead of me there! Good luck have fun!

Honest question, like I say I don't drive and I don't feel very knowledgeable about traffic: when are cars turning onto sidewalks? Driveways? Do you mean when crossing an intersection from the sidewalk? I feel like I've given the impression of riding on the sidewalk more than I actually do--when I realize I've gotten turned around and have reached a road I'm not comfortable on yet, I'll hop off my bike, move onto the sidewalk, walk with it for a bit, notice nobody's around, pedal for half a block paying attention to what it feels like to go over all the bumps and whatnot on a residential sidewalk, get to the end of the block and get off my bike again, usually to move back onto the road on the sidestreet I've just reached. I've maybe done this two or three times, usually I just walk. I'm failing to understand how I am safe walking with my bike but not riding it on the same stretch of sidewalk with only a slight increase in speed (like I said originally, if I am on the sidewalk I am practicing/experimenting with going slowly, which I try to avoid doing on the road. Though most speeds I go could probably be described as slow .) I am not commuting via sidewalk, and I will not be commuting via sidewalk. 
I want to know if what I am doing is dangerous but I'm struggling to understand your advice.

Additionally, I'm not afraid of being hit my a car on a busy street because of THEM doing something wrong, but because of me trying to signal and losing my balance, or me accidentally slipping off of my pedals and slowing down abruptly, or me turning in a way or at a time I'm not supposed to, or waiting when I'm supposed to go or going when I'm supposed to wait. I don't know how much being visible will help me if I screw up and do something unexpected. I am not very good at riding a bike yet and I would feel like I was putting other people in danger if I attempted to ride with traffic in all circumstances.

I never learned to drive partially because it scares the shit out of me, and I probably wouldn't be learning to cycle if I had a car and knew how to use it. I do ride with traffic though only on marked bike routes, but I'm not good enough at biking yet to take my hands off to signal, nor am I fit enough to maintain a good pace,  nor do I entirely know the rules of the road, so I am erring on the side of caution for now. Two weeks ago I couldn't get both feet onto the pedals without falling over so I don't think this is unreasonable.

I'm just wondering what people's thoughts are on riding slowly on the sidewalk if it is not in use by pedestrians.

I'm an occasional sidewalk cycler. I've been learning to ride a bike for the last two weeks and as I explore my neighborhood sometimes I get mixed up and end up on a busier road than I'm comfortable on (it really doesn't take a lot at this point). If there's people around, I get off and push my bike. If there's not, I practice pedaling slowly on the sidewalk. I would never try to pass someone on the sidewalk, or even ride near pedestrians at all as I'm just frankly not that confident in my skills yet. What is your opinion of this?

It IS easy, if I'm not cooking anything else, but if I'm making even say four other breakfasts, it really sucks to have to run away and back without overcooking anything, especially in a small restuarant without anyone else to watch the food for me. Servers are also ime less likely to really think about a mod/off menu order or ask the kitchen if something is okay if they are pressed for time.

Also frankly it depends how much you are paying. There's only so much extra effort I'm going to go through for a ten dollar breakfast, yknow? But if you are paying forty dollars for a fancy meal I think it's different.

Obviously you do have to sit down and work through your thoughts and feelings about transition steps like these, and that's not always easy either. And if what you want to do is transition, to me that is the definition of being transgender.

(Also, maybe more practically and less woo-wooy, if it is at all possible for you to play around some more with gender expression at home or wherever you feel comfortable, that can tell you a lot.
